chapter: Growing up with jazz in Belfast
title: Jimmy Compton's Belfast Dixieland band and its members
summary: Belfast's small wartime jazz scene, the polite society band, its members, and the dance jobs it played.

story.theme_name: Dance halls, lake camps and riverboat bandstands
story.community_name: Dance halls, lake resorts and where bands played

blocks.x: Uh-huh. Uh-huh. Uh, about the jazz in Ireland, do they have the same sort of set up that I read about and hear about in England, you know, little clubs where they, uh...

Well, not... You know what I mean? Yeah. Not... Not when I left. It wasn't as impressive as it was in London. One or two jobs, one or two little bands. The... At the time when I was in high school, and I left high school in 51, uh, they only had, to my knowledge, they only had, uh, Ken Smiley's band. And he left around that time and it was taken over by the trombone player, very good trombone player, called Jimmy Compton, and, uh, he was, uh, he's kept the band going and it's still playing now, to my knowledge. I can't think of any reason why it shouldn't, uh, why it shouldn't still be going. He was, of course, there was the same thing, Smiley and all were kind of high-class people, you know, they wore blazers and that, old-school blazers and nice accents and all, you know, and, uh...
Nothing dirty? Did they play any dirty type music?

No, no, more smooth. He liked to croon and that a little, you know, but it was like those Muggsy records. And then the trombone player was very like, I'm reminded of a parallel, it was very like the way The Last Straws is going now. This band I've been playing in, uh, they've been publicized as a society band and they've certainly got all their jobs as a society band through contacts rather than ability, I would say. I would suggest I don't, uh... And gradually the peasants are taking over. You see, the sort of people who I would say can play better but haven't got the social context and that's exactly what happened to, uh, uh, Ken Smiley's band. The tromboneist's name was Jimmy Compton. Now it's called Jimmy Compton. It's a Duxy Lion Pine. That's the way they talk over there. He had this pianist who's, uh, the pianist was a very good fella too. He was in the regular army in charge of training, uh, cadets. He got posted somewhere in England. And his pianist, this fella called Hoppy, uh, Hoppy Compton. And he was the fella who came to me and, uh, told me he wanted to be a trumpeter and play like Bix once. And I asked him, well, how was he getting on? I mean, what kind of trumpet did he have? He says, well, he didn't have a trumpet but, uh, it was a question of mind over matter. He said that, uh, Ravel and Tabusi were Bix's favorite, uh, composers and he was stashing up every Ravel and Tabusi disc he could lay his hands on. He was, that's about the angle, you know, but they, they had, it was a pretty good band.
You gotta have some kind of, you gotta have some kind of.
Sure, that was his idea. He played, he played very good piano but he was anxious to be refined about it, you know.
Was he the, uh, trombone player's brother?

That was it, that's right. Oh, it's a good band, it's still going, they play all kinds of jobs and they'll play, the idea with them was, I mean, they were a Dixieland band but they played sambas and rumbas and all the rest of it, whatever the dancers wanted. Which is what a real new audience band does, of course, I mean, whatever the music, whatever

the audience wants. They play for dancing and if it happens to come out of Dixieland, well, okay. That's right. If it doesn't, okay, you can still dance to it. But they, but it was, what, a six or seven piece of band?
That's right, seven, they had a guitar. Yeah. And the regular six, they didn't have a banjo.
